flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: List TCP's five guarantees and the mechanism behind each.
flashcards.a: Ordered delivery (sequence numbers), reliability (ACK + retransmission), flow control (receiver-advertised rwnd), congestion control (cwnd via slow start then congestion avoidance), and connection state (explicit handshake/teardown).

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.a: Only a checksum (optional in IPv4, mandatory in IPv6) and port-based demultiplexing. No ordering, no retransmission, no connection state, no congestion control.

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: What does TCP's 3-way handshake cost in RTTs, and what shaves it off?
flashcards.a: 1 RTT before any data flows normally. TCP Fast Open (RFC 7413) lets a returning client send data on the initial SYN using a cookie from a prior connection, skipping that RTT for repeat connections.

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: Why is UDP the right choice for RTP/video calls, with a number?
flashcards.a: Jitter buffers tolerate ~20-60ms; a single TCP retransmit round trip on a 100ms-RTT path already blows that budget, producing a multi-hundred-ms perceptible stall versus UDP's imperceptible dropped-frame concealment.

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: Where does head-of-line blocking occur in TCP, HTTP/2, and QUIC?
flashcards.a: TCP: connection-scoped, one lost segment blocks all later bytes. HTTP/2-over-TCP: inherits TCP's connection-scoped blocking across all multiplexed streams. QUIC: shrinks the scope to the STREAM -- a lost packet stalls only its own stream, but a stream itself is still ordered, so it's still blocked within itself.

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: Why does QUIC run over UDP instead of being its own IP protocol?
flashcards.a: Ossification: a genuinely new IP-layer protocol would be dropped by middleboxes/NATs/firewalls that only recognize TCP and UDP, and would require an OS kernel upgrade on every endpoint. UDP is already universally passable, so QUIC implements everything else (reliability, congestion control, encryption) in userspace libraries that ship at application-release speed.

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: What lets a QUIC connection survive a client's IP address changing (Wi-Fi to cellular)?
flashcards.a: QUIC identifies a connection by a Connection ID chosen at handshake time, not by the traditional 4-tuple (src/dst IP+port). TCP has no equivalent -- a TCP connection IS the 4-tuple.

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: What's the real cost QUIC pays for moving reliability and crypto to userspace?
flashcards.a: CPU: loss recovery and encryption that used to be kernel/NIC-offloaded work now run in the application process -- a measured, real overhead that drove staged rollout and NIC-level QUIC offload development rather than an overnight cutover.

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: When does DNS fall back from UDP to TCP?
flashcards.a: When the response would be truncated (server sets the TC bit) -- typically large record sets, DNSSEC-signed responses, or zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR, TCP-only by spec). A query fits in one UDP packet in the common case: <=512 bytes without EDNS0, up to 4096 with it negotiated.

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: What is a raw IP socket and who uses one?
flashcards.a: SOCK_RAW, requires CAP_NET_RAW/root; bypasses the kernel's TCP/UDP demultiplexing to construct/inspect IP packets directly. Used by ping/traceroute (ICMP), packet crafting tools (scapy, hping3), and protocols that run directly over IP with no port (OSPF, protocol number 89). Not an application-layer tool.

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: TCP congestion control: describe cwnd growth.
flashcards.a: Slow start: exponential growth, roughly doubling per RTT until ssthresh. Congestion avoidance: linear growth, +1 MSS per RTT after that. Shrinks on detected loss (fast retransmit / RTO).

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: Does QUIC eliminate head-of-line blocking entirely?
flashcards.a: No -- it shrinks the scope from the connection to the stream. A single stream is still an ordered byte sequence, so a lost packet on that stream still blocks later bytes of THAT stream from delivery; other streams are unaffected.

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: Name the specific RFCs for TCP, UDP, QUIC transport, QUIC+TLS, and HTTP/3.
flashcards.a: RFC 793 (TCP), RFC 768 (UDP), RFC 9000 (QUIC transport), RFC 9001 (Using TLS to Secure QUIC), RFC 9114 (HTTP/3).

flashcards.topic: TCP vs UDP vs IP vs QUIC
flashcards.q: Retryable errors vs non-retryable at the network layer -- how does idempotency interact with retry safety across TCP/UDP/QUIC transports?
flashcards.a: Transport reliability (TCP/QUIC's ACK+retransmit) is orthogonal to application-level idempotency. Even a fully reliable transport can deliver a request twice from the application's perspective (client-side timeout ambiguity), so a non-idempotent operation (e.g. POST) still needs an idempotency key regardless of which transport carries it.
